## 1.1 Purpose of institutional architecture
Institutional architecture explains how an organization fulfils its mandate through capabilities, responsibilities, information, services and relationships. Its subject is the institution’s ability to act coherently. Applications and infrastructure are important implementations, but neither the presence of software nor the number of platforms establishes that coherence.
This chapter establishes the foundation for the ZAF library. It defines the decisions that precede engineering architecture and the evidence needed to carry them into Book II. It is a working draft for review. It does not assert that the whole ZAF collection is complete, externally reviewed or adopted by an institution.
The question is not “what system should we buy?” The question is “what must this institution be able to do, under whose authority, with which information, and with what accountability when the normal process fails?”

## 1.2 The architecture mandate
An architecture mandate authorizes a defined scope of analysis and decision support. It names the sponsor, institutional boundary, decision rights, access constraints and expected work products. It must distinguish recommendation from authority: an architect may recommend a delegation model without possessing the legal or organizational power to grant that delegation.
| Mandate field | Required decision | Evidence to retain |
| Sponsor | Who authorizes the architecture work? | Recorded sponsorship and escalation route |
| Scope | Which institution, service or cross-institution journey is included? | Boundary statement and exclusions |
| Decision rights | Who accepts policy, risk and investment decisions? | Named decision owners and delegates |
| Access | Which records, staff and environments may be examined? | Authorized assessment boundary |
| Deliverables | Which decisions and artifacts will the work support? | Agreed work-product register |
| Acceptance | Who reviews factual accuracy and who accepts recommendations? | Review and acceptance responsibilities |
An architecture mandate is not a permission to perform intrusive testing, copy every database or publish institutional material. Discovery and publication require their own authorized boundaries. Where authority is unclear, record the open question and the decision it prevents.

## 1.3 Institutional promise and measurable outcomes
The institutional promise states what stakeholders should be able to rely on. It should be understandable without naming a product. In an operational approval service, the promise may be that an accepted request has an identifiable origin, an authorized decision, an explainable state and a route for correction or recovery.
Translate that promise into observable outcomes. Separate the citizen or staff outcome from the technical service measure. A two-second interface response does not prove that an application was resolved fairly or within the institution’s decision period. Equally, a policy delay should not be hidden inside a software availability metric.
| Outcome question | Candidate evidence | Interpretation limit |
| Can the applicant learn the authoritative state? | Journey walkthrough and state history | A sample does not prove every service behaves the same way |
| Can a reviewer explain the decision? | Linked version, authority and reason | A status label alone is insufficient |
| Can a disputed record be corrected lawfully? | Defined amendment and review path | Engineering cannot invent the governing policy |
| Can service resume after interruption? | Exercised continuity procedure | A configured backup is not a demonstrated recovery |
The owner decides acceptable targets after impact, cost and operating capability are examined. Do not attach impressive percentages to an institution that has not measured a baseline.

## 1.4 Institution, ecosystem and boundary
The institution is not identical to its application estate. It includes people, policies, funding, delegated powers, information ownership, partners and manual work. A process that depends on a telephone confirmation or a paper register belongs in the assessment even when it has no API.
Identify the system of interest at the appropriate scale. A single department, an institution-wide platform and a national ecosystem require different decision rights. Extending a local design into a multi-institution platform introduces authority and agreement questions that capacity planning alone cannot answer.
{{figure:institution}}
The view distinguishes the institutional mandate from domain responsibilities and enabling engineering. It is conceptual: it does not prescribe separate services, teams or physical infrastructure. Its value is to make the responsibility boundary visible before products are selected.

## 1.5 Stakeholders, concerns and authority
A stakeholder register is useful when it connects a person or role to a concern and an actual decision. “Management” is too broad when several authorities disagree. Record who uses the service, who owns its rules, who operates it, who is affected by its failure and who may challenge the outcome.
| Stakeholder | Concern to investigate | Decision or contribution |
| Service users | Access, clarity, cost of failure and correction | Validate the complete journey |
| Business owner | Mandate, authority and intended outcome | Approve business meaning and scope |
| Data owner | Meaning, permitted use and retention | Approve definitions and information boundaries |
| System owner | Operability, support and recovery | Accept operating responsibility |
| Risk or policy authority | Residual exposure and governing obligations | Accept treatment or require a change |
| Delivery team | Feasibility, dependencies and verification | Produce implementation evidence |
The register does not imply that one person must fill each role. Small teams may combine duties, while still making conflicts and critical independent checks explicit. A blank responsibility is an unresolved risk, not an implicit assignment to a supplier.

## 1.6 Capabilities, services and value streams
A capability describes what the institution must be able to do. A service presents a usable outcome to a stakeholder. A value stream connects activities that deliver that outcome. Keeping these concepts distinct avoids naming every screen as a capability or treating an organizational chart as the architecture.
For an approval journey, capabilities may include receiving requests, evaluating eligibility, authorizing action, executing it and reconciling the result. The service is the complete experience of obtaining and understanding a decision. Shared identity or notification supports that service but does not own its policy.
Document the successful path, rejection, withdrawal, amendment and interruption. A beautiful diagram of the happy path can hide the situations where institutional trust is actually tested.

## 1.7 Ownership and the operating model
Institutional architecture assigns authority over facts and decisions. If two systems can independently declare the same request approved, the issue is not merely duplication of storage: the institution has competing authorities. Name the owner of the authoritative fact and define how copies, projections and corrections relate to it.
The operating model explains how responsibilities cooperate. Shared capabilities should reduce repeated effort without taking over every domain decision. Domain autonomy should support change without allowing incompatible meanings or unaccountable exceptions.
| Architectural distinction | Institution-level decision | Engineering consequence |
| Authoritative fact versus copy | Who owns meaning and correction? | Source identifiers, versions and lineage |
| Common capability versus local policy | Which rules are shared? | Platform contract and domain boundary |
| Delegated action versus unrestricted access | Who may act, where and until when? | Scoped authorization and access lifecycle |
| Service outcome versus component health | What must users rely on? | User-journey signals and operating response |

## 1.8 Evidence, assumptions and institutional assessment
Separate observation, testimony, assumption and recommendation. A user complaint is evidence of an experienced problem; it is not automatically proof of its technical cause. A sampled contradiction is a finding within that sample; it is not a measured institution-wide failure rate.
Maintain an evidence register with source, date or period, access boundary, interpretation and uncertainty. Preserve only the material required for the agreed purpose. Redacted traces and approved samples may be enough; large uncontrolled exports increase risk without necessarily improving the decision.
A proposed future state should explain which finding or goal it addresses. If a component cannot be linked to a responsibility, concern or scenario, challenge its inclusion.

## 1.9 Institutional principles
Principles should constrain decisions rather than praise every possible solution. Each principle needs a rationale, an implementation consequence and an exception route.
| Principle | Institutional meaning | Decision consequence |
| Purpose before technology | Capabilities and mandate govern investments | Products are selected after requirements and ownership |
| One authority for each fact | Meaning and correction have an accountable owner | Copies disclose source and freshness |
| Explicit responsibility | Trust depends on known decision and service owners | Critical boundaries cannot remain unassigned |
| Local reality before imported complexity | Connectivity, staffing and continuity matter | Architecture fits the environment that will operate it |
| Evidence before a maturity claim | Installed components do not prove outcomes | Acceptance requires observed behaviour |
| Evolution with preserved rationale | Future teams need the reasons for present choices | Decisions retain alternatives, consequences and review triggers |
These are draft ZAF principles for examination, not universal rules imposed on every organization. An adopting institution must decide their applicability and approval mechanism.

## 1.10 Worked institutional example
Consider a fictional regional institution with a headquarters, six offices and a small engineering team. Its operational requests move through spreadsheets, email approval and manual reporting. The illustrative problem is the inability to connect fulfilment confidently to the exact authorized request version.
The institutional recommendation is to establish authoritative approval, ownership of execution facts and agreed reporting definitions. It is not yet a recommendation to deploy Kubernetes or Kafka. Those decisions belong to Book II after the operating constraints and architectural needs are established.
| Record | Institutional finding or decision | Next evidence |
| OBS-01 | Different reference conventions are a constructed scenario finding | Compare permitted source samples in a real assessment |
| DEC-01 | One owner must approve the request’s meaning and lifecycle | Named owner and agreed transitions |
| DEC-02 | Final approval remains online in the initial example | Business acceptance of waiting during interruption |
| OPEN-01 | Recovery target is not yet an institutional commitment | Impact assessment and tested feasibility |
The example demonstrates reasoning, not client delivery. No actual institution, efficiency gain, fraud reduction or operating result is claimed.

## 1.11 Institutional risks and unresolved decisions
Important uncertainties should be visible before engineering begins. Data placement, retention, delegated authority, interruption tolerance, supplier responsibility and funding for operation may materially change the feasible solution.
A risk register links cause, consequence, evidence, treatment and acceptance authority. Prioritization should consider harm and uncertainty. A high-risk unknown can justify a discovery task before a large implementation commitment.
Do not accept a risk on behalf of the institution merely because an implementation is technically possible. The architect records consequences and alternatives; the authorized owner accepts the residual exposure.

## 1.12 The institutional architecture artifact package
| Artifact ID | Work product | Acceptance evidence |
| ZAF-I-01-A01 | Architecture mandate | Scope, authority and review responsibilities recorded |
| ZAF-I-01-A02 | Stakeholder and concern register | Material concerns have owners and decision routes |
| ZAF-I-01-A03 | Institutional promise and outcome scenarios | Outcomes distinguish user, policy and technical concerns |
| ZAF-I-01-A04 | Capability and responsibility map | No critical decision or fact has competing unexplained authority |
| ZAF-I-01-A05 | Evidence and uncertainty register | Findings are traceable and limitations are visible |
| ZAF-I-01-A06 | Principles and institutional decision log | Rationale, alternatives and review triggers retained |
These identifiers support later cross-references. A project may tailor the package, but it should record why an artifact is unnecessary rather than silently omitting the responsibility it represents.

## 1.13 Handoff to Book II — Engineering Architecture
Book II consumes the accepted institutional decisions and translates them into reference architectures, technology standards, platform contracts and engineering responsibilities. It does not replace the institutional mandate or invent missing policy.
{{figure:handoff}}
| Institutional input | Book II response | Verification question |
| Approved capability and owner | Reference architecture and domain responsibilities | Does the technical boundary preserve authority? |
| Information policy and source meaning | Enterprise data and security architecture | Can a projection be traced and corrected appropriately? |
| Continuity and operating constraints | Infrastructure, network and operations architecture | Can the actual team operate and recover it? |
| Governance and exception rules | Technology governance and architecture decisions | Are changes reviewable and reversible where required? |
A technology chapter can be conditional. The dedicated Kubernetes architecture section belongs in Book II, while its applicability must follow an approved adoption decision. The existence of the chapter does not mandate Kubernetes for every engagement.

## 1.14 Review checklist for this draft
- The institution and assessment boundary are explicit.
- Mandate, recommendation and approval authority are distinguished.
- Stakeholder concerns connect to decisions rather than generic role lists.
- Capabilities and information have accountable owners.
- Rejected, amended and interrupted journeys are included.
- Findings distinguish evidence from assumptions.
- Technology selection does not precede institutional decisions.
- Unresolved risks have owners and required next evidence.
- Artifacts have stable identifiers and review responsibility.
- Book II receives explicit institutional inputs.
This is a review checklist, not evidence that a particular institution has passed it. Review results should identify the version examined, reviewer, scope, findings and disposition.

## 1.15 Decisions required before advancing
The editor and adopting organization should resolve the scope of the institutional model, confirm the next section’s concerns and review this draft’s terminology. A draft becomes accepted only through the library’s documented review process; publishing it on the website does not constitute approval.
The next Book I section is Institutional Context & Stakeholder Concerns. It should extend the mandate into a documented context model, concern register, viewpoints and a discovery plan. Engineering implementation remains outside this first section’s acceptance claim.
body.fr:
## 1.1 Finalité de l’architecture institutionnelle
L’architecture institutionnelle explique comment une organisation accomplit son mandat à travers capacités, responsabilités, information, services et relations. Les logiciels sont des réalisations possibles ; leur présence ne prouve pas la cohérence de l’institution.
Cette section fonde la bibliothèque ZAF et les décisions qui précèdent le Livre II. Elle est un brouillon de travail. Elle ne déclare ni l’achèvement des huit livres, ni une revue externe, ni une adoption institutionnelle.
La question initiale est : que doit accomplir l’institution, sous quelle autorité, avec quelles informations et quelle responsabilité en cas d’échec ?

## 1.2 Mandat d’architecture
Le mandat définit sponsor, périmètre, autorité, accès et livrables. L’architecte recommande une délégation sans posséder nécessairement le pouvoir de l’accorder.
| Élément | Décision | Preuve conservée |
| Sponsor | Autorité qui engage le travail | Sponsorship et escalade |
| Périmètre | Institution, service ou parcours concerné | Frontières et exclusions |
| Droits de décision | Autorité des politiques, risques et investissements | Responsables et délégations |
| Accès | Données, personnes et environnements autorisés | Périmètre d’évaluation |
| Livrables | Décisions soutenues par le travail | Registre des pièces attendues |
| Acceptation | Validation des faits et des recommandations | Responsabilités de revue |
Le mandat n’autorise pas automatiquement des tests intrusifs, des exports complets ou la publication de données institutionnelles. Toute autorité incertaine reste une question ouverte.

## 1.3 Promesse et résultats institutionnels
La promesse décrit ce sur quoi les acteurs doivent pouvoir compter, sans nommer un produit. Pour un service d’approbation, une demande acceptée possède une origine, une décision autorisée, un état explicable et une voie de correction ou de reprise.
Séparer résultat utilisateur, décision métier et mesure technique. Une interface rapide ne prouve pas une décision juste ou rendue dans le délai institutionnel.
| Question | Preuve candidate | Limite |
| État faisant autorité accessible ? | Parcours et historique | L’échantillon ne prouve pas tous les services |
| Décision explicable ? | Version, autorité et motif | Un statut seul est insuffisant |
| Correction permise ? | Circuit d’amendement | L’ingénierie ne crée pas la politique |
| Reprise possible ? | Exercice vérifié | Sauvegarde configurée différente de reprise démontrée |
Les objectifs chiffrés suivent analyse d’impact, coûts et capacité d’exploitation. Ils ne doivent pas être inventés avant mesure.

## 1.4 Institution et écosystème
L’institution comprend personnes, politiques, financement, délégations, propriétaires d’information, partenaires et tâches manuelles. Un registre papier ou un appel de confirmation appartient au fonctionnement réel.
Une architecture de service, d’institution et d’écosystème national exige des autorités différentes. La capacité technique ne résout pas seule la coopération entre institutions.
{{figure:institution}}
Cette vue sépare mandat, responsabilités métier et réalisation technique. Elle ne prescrit ni microservices ni équipes distinctes.

## 1.5 Acteurs, préoccupations et autorité
Un registre relie acteur, préoccupation et décision. « Direction » ne suffit pas lorsque plusieurs autorités divergent.
| Acteur | Préoccupation | Contribution |
| Utilisateurs | Accès, clarté et correction | Valider le parcours complet |
| Responsable métier | Mandat et résultat | Approuver le sens et le périmètre |
| Propriétaire des données | Sens, usage et conservation | Approuver les définitions |
| Responsable système | Exploitation et reprise | Accepter la responsabilité opérationnelle |
| Autorité des risques | Exposition résiduelle | Accepter ou imposer un traitement |
| Équipe de réalisation | Faisabilité et vérification | Produire les preuves techniques |
Plusieurs rôles peuvent être réunis, mais conflits et contrôles critiques restent explicites. Une responsabilité vide ne se transfère pas implicitement au fournisseur.

## 1.6 Capacités, services et chaînes de valeur
Une capacité décrit ce que l’institution sait accomplir. Un service présente un résultat utilisable. Une chaîne de valeur relie les activités nécessaires. Un écran n’est donc pas automatiquement une capacité.
Pour une approbation : recevoir, examiner, autoriser, exécuter et rapprocher. Identité et notification soutiennent le parcours sans posséder sa politique. Documenter aussi refus, retrait, amendement et interruption.

## 1.7 Responsabilité et modèle de fonctionnement
Si deux systèmes peuvent déclarer indépendamment la même demande approuvée, l’institution possède des autorités concurrentes. Nommer le propriétaire du fait et les relations entre copies, projections et corrections.
| Distinction | Décision institutionnelle | Conséquence technique |
| Référence et copie | Propriété du sens et de la correction | Identifiants, versions et traçabilité |
| Capacité commune et règle locale | Règles partagées | Contrats plateforme et frontières métier |
| Délégation et accès général | Qui agit, où et jusqu’à quand ? | Autorisation limitée et cycle des accès |
| Résultat et santé des composants | Promesse aux utilisateurs | Signaux de parcours et réponse opérationnelle |
Le partage doit réduire la duplication sans absorber toutes les décisions métier. L’autonomie doit préserver des règles cohérentes.

## 1.8 Preuves et hypothèses
Distinguer observation, témoignage, hypothèse et recommandation. Une plainte indique un problème vécu sans prouver sa cause technique. Une contradiction dans un échantillon ne représente pas un taux global.
Conserver source, période, autorisation, interprétation et incertitude. Minimiser les copies. Chaque élément cible doit répondre à un objectif, un constat ou une responsabilité.

## 1.9 Principes institutionnels
| Principe | Sens | Conséquence |
| Finalité avant technologie | Le mandat gouverne l’investissement | Produits après exigences et responsabilités |
| Une autorité par fait | Correction attribuée | Copies avec source et fraîcheur |
| Responsabilité explicite | Confiance attribuable | Aucun service critique sans responsable |
| Réalité locale | Réseau et personnel comptent | Complexité adaptée à l’exploitation |
| Preuve avant maturité annoncée | Installation différente de résultat | Acceptation par comportement observé |
| Évolution avec justification | Préserver les raisons | Options, conséquences et déclencheurs conservés |
Ces principes sont proposés pour revue. Une institution adopte leur applicabilité et son mécanisme d’exception.

## 1.10 Exemple institutionnel
Une institution fictive possède un siège, six antennes et une petite équipe technique. Tableurs, emails et rapports manuels ne permettent pas de relier sûrement l’exécution à la version autorisée.
La recommandation institutionnelle consiste à établir approbation faisant autorité, propriété des faits d’exécution et définitions du reporting. Kafka ou Kubernetes ne sont pas encore décidés.
| Référence | Constat ou décision | Prochaine preuve |
| OBS-01 | Conventions différentes dans le scénario construit | Échantillons autorisés |
| DEC-01 | Un propriétaire du cycle de demande | Responsable et transitions convenus |
| DEC-02 | Approbation finale en ligne au départ | Acceptation de l’attente pendant coupure |
| OPEN-01 | Objectif de reprise non engagé | Impact et faisabilité testée |
Cet exemple n’est pas une réalisation client et ne revendique aucun gain mesuré.

## 1.11 Risques et décisions ouvertes
Localisation, conservation, délégation, interruption tolérable, fournisseur et financement opérationnel peuvent modifier la solution. Les rendre visibles avant réalisation.
Le registre relie cause, conséquence, preuve, traitement et autorité d’acceptation. Une inconnue critique peut justifier de la découverte avant investissement. L’architecte ne doit pas accepter le risque à la place de l’autorité institutionnelle.

## 1.12 Pièces d’architecture
| Identifiant | Pièce | Preuve d’acceptation |
| ZAF-I-01-A01 | Mandat | Périmètre et autorités enregistrés |
| ZAF-I-01-A02 | Registre des acteurs | Préoccupations et décisions attribuées |
| ZAF-I-01-A03 | Promesse et scénarios | Résultats utilisateur, métier et techniques distingués |
| ZAF-I-01-A04 | Capacités et responsabilités | Autorité critique non concurrente |
| ZAF-I-01-A05 | Preuves et incertitudes | Constats traçables et limites visibles |
| ZAF-I-01-A06 | Principes et décisions | Justifications et révisions conservées |
Une adaptation du dossier doit expliquer les omissions plutôt que masquer la responsabilité correspondante.

## 1.13 Passage au Livre II
Le Livre II transforme les décisions institutionnelles acceptées en architectures de référence, standards technologiques et responsabilités d’ingénierie. Il ne remplace pas le mandat.
{{figure:handoff}}
| Entrée institutionnelle | Réponse du Livre II | Question |
| Capacité et propriétaire | Architecture de référence | Autorité préservée ? |
| Politique d’information | Architecture données et sécurité | Traçabilité et correction possibles ? |
| Continuité et exploitation | Infrastructure et opérations | Équipe capable de reprendre ? |
| Gouvernance | Décisions technologiques | Changements révisables ? |
Le chapitre Kubernetes du Livre II est conservé. Son applicabilité suit une décision d’adoption ; son existence ne l’impose pas à chaque projet.

## 1.14 Liste de revue
- Périmètre explicite.
- Mandat, recommandation et approbation distingués.
- Préoccupations reliées aux décisions.
- Propriétaires des capacités et informations nommés.
- Parcours refusés, modifiés et interrompus inclus.
- Preuves distinctes des hypothèses.
- Choix technologiques après décisions institutionnelles.
- Risques et prochaines preuves attribués.
- Pièces identifiées et révisables.
- Entrées du Livre II explicites.
Cette liste ne prouve pas une conformité institutionnelle. Enregistrer version, réviseur, périmètre, constats et décisions de traitement.

## 1.15 Décision avant progression
La prochaine section est Contexte institutionnel et préoccupations des acteurs. Elle développe modèle de contexte, registre des préoccupations et plan de découverte.
La publication de ce brouillon ne constitue pas son acceptation. Le passage à un statut accepté suit le processus de revue documenté dans la bibliothèque.

## 2.1 Purpose and decisions supported
Institutional context is the set of relationships, obligations, operating conditions and stakeholder concerns that makes an architecture decision meaningful. A context model explains what the institution is responsible for, what depends on others and which uncertainties can change the proposed solution. It is a decision instrument, not a decorative diagram around an application.
This section turns the mandate developed in Section 01 into a scoped context model, a stakeholder and concern register, a set of useful viewpoints and an evidence-collection plan. Section 01 remains a working draft: its assumptions are inputs to examine, not silently approved institutional policy. This section also remains a draft until the required review and acceptance process is recorded.
The first decisions supported are the assessment boundary, the people who must participate, the concerns the architecture must address and the evidence required before recommending a target.

## 2.2 Inputs, authority and assessment boundary
Begin with the architecture mandate, the institutional promise, a candidate service journey and the current decision-owner list. Record the version of each input. An unresolved authority question in Section 01 must stay visible in this section rather than being converted into an assumed permission.
| Input | Context question | Treatment if missing |
| Mandate and sponsor | Who authorizes the work and its limits? | Record an open mandate decision; restrict discovery to permitted activity |
| Service or capability scope | What outcome and journey are included? | Agree a bounded journey before inventorying everything |
| Institutional owners | Who decides meaning, use, risk and investment? | Identify roles and confirm actual authority |
| Operating constraints | Which conditions can invalidate the target? | Mark assumptions and plan representative evidence |
| Access conditions | What may be interviewed, inspected or tested? | Establish authorization and handling rules |
The boundary should distinguish the organization of interest, the service of interest and the technical systems that support it. These boundaries may overlap without being identical. A shared identity provider is a technical dependency; it does not necessarily own the institution’s approval authority.

## 2.3 Context dimensions
A context assessment should examine more than the software estate. The dimensions below are discovery prompts, not a requirement to collect unlimited information.
| Dimension | Questions to resolve | Candidate evidence |
| Mandate and policy | Which authority governs the service and exceptions? | Approved mandate, policy and delegation records |
| Organizational | Which units perform, approve and support the work? | Responsibility map and end-to-end walkthrough |
| Service and user | What result is needed, including rejection and correction? | Representative journeys and user testimony |
| Information | Which facts are authoritative and who may correct them? | Definitions, source samples and retention decisions |
| Ecosystem | Which partners, suppliers and institutions influence the result? | Contracts, dependencies and support agreements |
| Operating environment | How do power, connectivity, staffing and language affect the journey? | Incident history and permitted observation |
| Change and resources | Which changes, budgets or deadlines constrain the decision? | Approved initiatives and available capacity |
Policy interpretation and legal applicability belong to the authorized institutional or specialist owner. The architecture records the requirement and its consequence; it does not manufacture legal authority from a technical preference.

## 2.4 Worked context and explicit exclusions
The continuing example is a fictional regional institution with a headquarters, six offices and a small engineering team. Requests are submitted locally, reviewed by a department, authorized by finance, fulfilled by operations and included in a consolidated report.
For this section, the assessment is limited to one request type and a candidate pilot office. Other offices matter as context and future consumers, not as evidence that the pilot represents the whole institution. The example’s conditions and findings are constructed to demonstrate the method.
| In the discovery boundary | Outside the initial boundary | Re-entry trigger |
| One operational approval journey | All institutional services | A separately authorized scope change |
| Request, decision, execution and report references | Full production-data replication | A justified and authorized evidence need |
| Roles affecting the selected journey | Complete HR or payroll review | A material dependency with explicit access |
| Connectivity and recovery constraints | A commitment to final offline approval | Approved continuity and conflict policy |
| Existing service dependencies | A national interoperability platform | A new institutional mandate |
Exclusions are not declarations that an area is unimportant. They make the scope, limitations and conditions for further work explicit.

## 2.5 Institutional context view
{{figure:context}}
The institution is the decision boundary in this view. Users initiate work and may challenge its outcome. Policy and risk owners authorize governing rules. External service providers have their own operating responsibility. Internal service owners remain accountable for decisions even when implementation is delegated.
Every crossing should identify the information exchanged, the authority retained, the service expectation and the failure response. An external provider may acknowledge delivery without establishing that an institutional approval was legitimate. Conversely, a valid internal decision can exist while its notification is delayed.
The diagram is a reference model. The identity provider, storage location, supplier and manual fallback are discovery questions until supported by evidence. No actual integration, hosting arrangement or institution-wide control is claimed.

## 2.6 Stakeholder identification and representation
Identify stakeholders by their relationship to the service and its consequences. Include requesters, frontline staff, delegated reviewers, execution teams, information owners, operators, risk owners, support staff and people responsible for correction or appeal.
Do not treat seniority as the only measure of importance. A person with little formal influence may experience most of the cost of a failed process. A sponsor’s approval does not remove the need to understand that experience. Representative participation should account for different offices, languages, accessibility needs, device conditions and unsuccessful journeys where relevant.
| Stakeholder ID | Role in the example | Concern to examine | Participation needed |
| ST-01 | Requester or authorized representative | Status, explanation and correction | Journey interview and review of an unsuccessful case |
| ST-02 | Frontline processing staff | Completeness, duplicate work and interruptions | Observed walkthrough within approved access |
| ST-03 | Department reviewer | Purpose, delegated authority and amended content | Policy and exception walkthrough |
| ST-04 | Finance owner | Authorized amounts and reporting meaning | Definition review and reconciliation sample |
| ST-05 | Operations owner | Acting on current authority | Fulfilment and cancellation walkthrough |
| ST-06 | Data steward and owner | Meaning, access and corrections | Source and information-policy review |
| ST-07 | System and support owner | Operability, incidents and recovery | Release, incident and restore walkthrough |
| ST-08 | Risk, policy or control owner | Residual exposure and traceability | Review of constraints and unresolved decisions |
These identifiers name roles in a fictional register. A real engagement records the actual representative, their authority, contact route and evidence of participation under the agreed information-handling rules.

## 2.7 Concern register: make each concern actionable
Register IDs ST-xx, C-xx, VP-xx and DEC-xx are local to ZAF-I-02. Cross-section references include the document prefix to avoid confusing them with another section’s records.
A concern is useful when it can change a decision, a requirement, an assessment activity or an acceptance scenario. “We need a modern platform” is not yet specific enough. Ask what is failing, who is affected, what consequence matters and which evidence would distinguish a useful change from an attractive product.
| Concern ID | Concern statement | Raised by | Decision influenced | Evidence required |
| C-01 | A requester cannot distinguish unsent work from an accepted request | ST-01, ST-02 | Receipt and state semantics | Interrupted submission walkthrough |
| C-02 | Approval may refer to content different from execution | ST-03, ST-05 | Version-bound authority | Trace an amendment through fulfilment |
| C-03 | Reports mix incompatible cut-offs | ST-04 | Reporting contract | Known-period reconciliation |
| C-04 | A branch cannot continue during a network interruption | ST-02, ST-07 | Continuity and offline policy | Outage conditions and business impact |
| C-05 | Correction could erase the original decision evidence | ST-06, ST-08 | Amendment and audit design | Policy and correction scenario |
| C-06 | Recovery is assumed but not demonstrated | ST-07, ST-08 | Recovery objectives and staffing | Authorized isolated restore |
Record the source and status of each concern. A concern raised in an interview is not automatically a confirmed finding. A resolved concern should link to the decision or evidence that supports closure.

## 2.8 Authority, influence and acceptance
For each material concern, distinguish who experiences it, who understands its causes, who can authorize a change and who will operate the result. These may be four different parties.
An engagement plan should specify how concerns are collected, how factual corrections are reviewed and how conflicting recommendations are escalated. Consultation is not the same as approval. Reviewing a diagram does not mean accepting its residual risks.
| Activity | Contribution | Authority retained |
| User review | Explain actual effort, failure and correction needs | Institutional policy remains with its authorized owner |
| Technical review | Assess feasibility and demonstrate behaviour | Technical feasibility does not approve institutional risk |
| Data review | Confirm definitions and information boundaries | Source correction follows the data owner’s authority |
| Executive decision | Select scope, funding and accepted exposure | Decision and rationale must be recorded |
If no authorized owner can be identified, mark the decision blocked. Do not solve the ownership gap by assigning it to whichever engineer is available.

## 2.9 Conflicting concerns and explicit trade-offs
Concern C-04 may favour uninterrupted local activity. Concern C-02 may favour centralized approval against the current version. Both are legitimate concerns; the architecture should expose the conflict rather than describe one as resistance to change.
| Conflict | Candidate option | Benefit | Consequence and decision owner |
| Continuity versus one authoritative approval | Preserve drafts offline; finalize online | Avoids independent final decisions | Branch waits during outage; business owner accepts continuity policy |
| Continuity versus one authoritative approval | Permit bounded offline decisions | Enables selected local actions | Requires delegation, conflict and reconciliation rules; policy and risk owners decide |
| Detailed traceability versus data minimization | Retain defined decision evidence with limited access | Supports explanation and review | Retention and access must be justified by data owner |
| Fast rollout versus recoverable operation | Pilot before broad expansion | Exposes failure modes at smaller scope | Initial coverage is limited; sponsor accepts sequence |
The recommendation in this example remains drafts offline and final approval online. It is conditional on business acceptance of the interruption cost. It is not a universal ZAF prohibition on offline approvals.
A decision record should retain the rejected options, assumptions and review trigger. If the institution later changes its delegation model or outage tolerance, the earlier decision can be reconsidered without pretending it was wrong under its original conditions.

## 2.10 Viewpoints and useful architecture views
Within this library, a viewpoint states which stakeholder concerns a view addresses, which modelling conventions it uses and what its reader should be able to decide. A view is the actual representation prepared for a defined scope. These are working editorial definitions for ZAF.
A single diagram cannot answer all institutional questions. Select a small set of complementary views and explain their limits.
| Viewpoint ID | Stakeholders and concerns | View to produce | Decision supported |
| VP-01 Context | Sponsor, service owners; scope and dependency | Institutional boundary with exchanges and external owners | Assessment and responsibility boundary |
| VP-02 Authority | Delegated owners; C-02 and C-05 | Journey, state and authority map | Valid decision and correction policy |
| VP-03 Information | Finance and data owners; C-03 and C-05 | Source, definition and reporting lineage | Meaning, correction and publication |
| VP-04 Continuity | Frontline and system owners; C-01, C-04 and C-06 | Interrupted journey and recovery responsibilities | Degraded operation and recovery targets |
| VP-05 Change | Sponsor and delivery owners; cost and feasibility | Dependencies, alternatives and transition gates | Safe investment sequence |
Each view identifies its subject, version, scope, legend, source, author, open questions and intended reviewers. A drawing without those boundaries may look authoritative while leaving its interpretation uncontrolled.

## 2.11 Traceability from concern to decision
{{figure:traceability}}
Maintain a traceable chain from stakeholder concern to evidence, requirement or decision, the view that explains it and the verification that would support acceptance. Traceability is not the number of links in a spreadsheet; it is the ability to answer why a recommendation exists and what would make it change.
| Concern | Evidence or unknown | Proposed decision | View | Verification |
| C-01 | Outcome uncertain after a lost response | DEC-01: stable command receipt and explicit pending state | VP-04 | Retry an ambiguous submission and inspect the original outcome |
| C-02 | Approved version not linked in the scenario | DEC-02: approval bound to the reviewed version | VP-02 | Reject a stale approval after an amendment |
| C-03 | Reporting cut-off unagreed | DEC-03: versioned reporting contract | VP-03 | Reconcile one permitted known period |
| C-06 | Restore duration unknown | DEC-04: agree objectives, then exercise recovery | VP-04 | Timed isolated restore with completeness checks |
A link to an unknown is useful if it clearly identifies what must be learned. It must not be presented as a completed verification.

## 2.12 Discovery and evidence-collection plan
Plan discovery around decisions, not around collecting the largest possible inventory. Use interviews to understand intended practice, observation to understand the actual journey and permitted records to test a claim. Triangulate important findings rather than treating one confident interview as a complete assessment.
| Activity | Purpose | Evidence handling | Output |
| Mandate workshop | Confirm authority and scope | Approved notes and decisions | Boundary and owner record |
| Journey walkthrough | Follow successful and unsuccessful work | Redacted or synthetic samples where sufficient | Journey and exception map |
| Source and report review | Explain one result end to end | Minimum permitted records with defined retention | Meaning and reconciliation notes |
| Dependency review | Identify supplier and support obligations | Contract extracts approved for the review | Dependency and escalation register |
| Continuity review | Establish actual interruption and recovery constraints | Authorized incident history and isolated exercises | Continuity assumptions and evidence gaps |
For each activity, identify the participant, authorization, expected evidence, handling rule, limitation and decision it supports. No intrusive test, secret collection or uncontrolled production export follows automatically from this plan.
Representative coverage is a design choice to justify. Record which offices and journeys were included, which were excluded and why. Avoid statistical claims when the evidence does not support them.

## 2.13 Uncertainty and change in context
Maintain a context-change register. A new provider, revised delegation, organizational restructuring, changed retention policy or more demanding service objective may invalidate an earlier recommendation.
| Context item | Current status in the example | Decision affected | Trigger for reassessment |
| Branch connectivity | Assumed interruptions; measurement pending | Offline continuity | Evidence differs materially from the assumed pattern |
| Engineering capacity | Small team assumed | Platform complexity | Support responsibility or staffing changes |
| Data placement | Institutional decision pending | Hosting and external dependencies | Approved information policy changes |
| Recovery objectives | Candidate values only | Backup and deployment design | Impact analysis or restore exercise changes feasibility |
Assign an owner to monitor each important trigger. “Review every year” may be useful as a backstop, but material change should not wait for the calendar.

## 2.14 Artifact package and review gate
| Artifact ID | Work product | Review evidence |
| ZAF-I-02-A01 | Context and scope model | Boundaries, exchanges, exclusions and external owners are explicit |
| ZAF-I-02-A02 | Stakeholder register | Material roles, representation and decision authority are identified |
| ZAF-I-02-A03 | Concern register | Concerns connect to decisions and distinguish testimony from confirmed findings |
| ZAF-I-02-A04 | Viewpoint and view catalog | Each view addresses named concerns and states its limits |
| ZAF-I-02-A05 | Discovery and evidence plan | Collection is authorized, proportionate and decision-led |
| ZAF-I-02-A06 | Conflict and decision register | Alternatives, consequences, owners and unresolved choices remain visible |
| ZAF-I-02-A07 | Context-change and dependency register | Reassessment triggers and accountable owners are recorded |
The review gate tests whether the institutional context is sufficient for the next decision. It does not require every unknown to disappear. Material unknowns must have an owner, a learning activity and a clear restriction on the decisions they block.

## 2.15 Review checklist and next section
- The context model distinguishes institutional, service and technical boundaries.
- In-scope and excluded activities are explicit.
- Affected users and frontline roles are represented alongside formal authorities.
- Material concerns identify their source, consequence and decision impact.
- Consultation, factual review and acceptance authority are distinguished.
- Conflicting concerns retain alternatives and an escalation owner.
- Every selected viewpoint addresses named concerns and has a usable legend and scope.
- Evidence collection is authorized, proportionate and limited.
- Assumptions and incomplete coverage are visible.
- Context-change triggers identify when recommendations must be reconsidered.
- Section 01 is referenced without falsely claiming it has been accepted.
- Artifacts have stable identifiers and required review evidence.
The next section is Institutional Purpose, Value & Public Outcomes. It will develop outcome definitions, value-stream reasoning and measurement boundaries using this context package. Section 02 remains a working draft; the editor must record the actual review scope, findings and disposition before any status promotion.

## 2.1 Objet et décisions soutenues
Le contexte institutionnel rassemble relations, obligations, conditions de fonctionnement et préoccupations qui donnent un sens à une décision d’architecture. Il explique ce que l’institution maîtrise, ce qui dépend d’autres acteurs et quelles inconnues peuvent modifier la solution.
Cette section transforme le mandat de la section 01 en modèle de contexte, registre des acteurs et préoccupations, points de vue et plan de collecte des preuves. La section 01 reste un brouillon : ses hypothèses ne deviennent pas des politiques approuvées. La présente section est également soumise à revue.
Les premières décisions concernent le périmètre, les participants, les préoccupations à traiter et les éléments à connaître avant de recommander une cible.

## 2.2 Entrées, autorité et périmètre
Commencer par mandat, promesse institutionnelle, parcours choisi et responsables. Identifier la version des entrées et conserver les questions d’autorité non résolues.
| Entrée | Question | Traitement si absente |
| Mandat et sponsor | Qui autorise le travail ? | Décision de mandat ouverte et découverte limitée |
| Service ou capacité | Quel résultat est inclus ? | Définir un parcours borné |
| Responsables | Qui décide du sens, du risque et de l’investissement ? | Confirmer les autorités réelles |
| Contraintes | Qu’est-ce qui peut invalider la cible ? | Hypothèses et preuves représentatives |
| Accès | Que peut-on examiner ou tester ? | Autorisation et règles de traitement |
Distinguer institution, service et systèmes techniques. Un fournisseur d’identité peut être une dépendance sans posséder l’autorité d’approbation.

## 2.3 Dimensions du contexte
Ces dimensions orientent la découverte sans justifier une collecte illimitée.
| Dimension | Questions | Preuves possibles |
| Mandat et politique | Autorité du service et des exceptions | Mandat et délégations |
| Organisation | Réalisation, approbation et support | Responsabilités et parcours |
| Utilisateur | Résultat, refus et correction | Témoignages et situations représentatives |
| Information | Source faisant autorité et correction | Définitions et échantillons autorisés |
| Écosystème | Partenaires et obligations | Contrats et dépendances |
| Exploitation | Réseau, énergie, personnel et langues | Historique et observation permise |
| Changement | Ressources et calendrier | Initiatives approuvées |
L’autorité institutionnelle ou spécialisée interprète les obligations applicables. L’architecte en documente les conséquences.

## 2.4 Exemple et exclusions
L’exemple fictif conserve un siège, six antennes et une petite équipe technique. La demande passe du dépôt à la revue, à l’autorisation financière, à l’exécution puis au rapport.
La découverte vise un type de demande et une antenne pilote candidate. Les autres antennes constituent le contexte, sans prouver que le pilote les représente.
| Inclus | Exclu au départ | Condition de réintégration |
| Un parcours d’approbation | Tous les services | Nouveau périmètre autorisé |
| Références de demande et d’exécution | Réplication complète de production | Besoin de preuve autorisé |
| Rôles du parcours | Audit RH ou paie complet | Dépendance pertinente et accès explicite |
| Contraintes de continuité | Approbation finale hors connexion | Politique de conflits approuvée |
| Dépendances existantes | Plateforme nationale | Nouveau mandat institutionnel |
Une exclusion rend la limite visible ; elle ne déclare pas le sujet sans importance.

## 2.5 Vue de contexte
{{figure:context}}
L’institution représente la frontière de décision. Les utilisateurs initient le travail et peuvent contester son résultat. Les responsables de politique et risques autorisent les règles. Les fournisseurs conservent leurs responsabilités opérationnelles ; les propriétaires internes restent responsables de leurs décisions.
Chaque échange précise information, autorité conservée, attente de service et réponse à l’échec. Un accusé de livraison ne prouve pas la validité d’une approbation ; une décision valide peut exister malgré un email retardé.
Cette vue reste illustrative. Identité, stockage, fournisseur et solution manuelle sont des questions de découverte tant que les preuves manquent.

## 2.6 Identification et représentation des acteurs
Identifier les acteurs par leur relation au service et aux conséquences : demandeurs, agents de terrain, approbateurs, opérateurs, responsables des données, exploitants et autorités de correction.
La hiérarchie n’est pas le seul critère. Un acteur peu influent peut supporter le coût principal d’un échec. Considérer antennes, langues, accessibilité, appareils et parcours refusés.
| ID | Rôle | Préoccupation | Participation |
| ST-01 | Demandeur ou représentant | État et correction | Entretien et cas non réussi |
| ST-02 | Agent de traitement | Complétude et interruption | Parcours observé autorisé |
| ST-03 | Responsable de service | Délégation et contenu modifié | Revue des règles et exceptions |
| ST-04 | Finance | Montants et sens du rapport | Définitions et rapprochement |
| ST-05 | Opérations | Autorisation actuelle | Exécution et annulation |
| ST-06 | Responsable des données | Sens et correction | Sources et politique |
| ST-07 | Système et support | Incidents et reprise | Versions et restauration |
| ST-08 | Risques, politique ou contrôle | Exposition et traçabilité | Contraintes et décisions ouvertes |
Dans une mission réelle, enregistrer représentant, autorité et preuve de participation selon les règles de traitement convenues.

## 2.7 Registre des préoccupations
Les identifiants ST-xx, C-xx, VP-xx et DEC-xx sont locaux à ZAF-I-02. Toute référence entre sections inclut ce préfixe documentaire.
Une préoccupation exploitable peut modifier une décision, une exigence ou une vérification. « Plateforme moderne » doit être traduit en problème, conséquence et preuve attendue.
| ID | Préoccupation | Acteurs | Décision | Preuve |
| C-01 | Brouillon non transmis confondu avec demande reçue | ST-01, ST-02 | Réception et états | Soumission interrompue |
| C-02 | Exécution différente de la version autorisée | ST-03, ST-05 | Approbation versionnée | Amendement suivi jusqu’à l’exécution |
| C-03 | Périodes de rapport incompatibles | ST-04 | Contrat de reporting | Période connue rapprochée |
| C-04 | Antenne bloquée par coupure | ST-02, ST-07 | Continuité | Conditions et impact |
| C-05 | Correction effaçant les preuves | ST-06, ST-08 | Amendement et audit | Politique et scénario |
| C-06 | Reprise supposée | ST-07, ST-08 | Objectifs de récupération | Restauration isolée |
Un entretien ne confirme pas automatiquement un constat. Toute clôture doit renvoyer à la décision ou preuve correspondante.

## 2.8 Autorité et acceptation
Distinguer qui vit le problème, qui en comprend les causes, qui peut autoriser un changement et qui exploitera le résultat.
| Activité | Contribution | Autorité conservée |
| Revue utilisateur | Effort, échec et correction | Politique auprès du responsable habilité |
| Revue technique | Faisabilité et comportement | Risque institutionnel non accepté par simple faisabilité |
| Revue données | Définitions et frontières | Correction selon l’autorité propriétaire |
| Décision exécutive | Périmètre et investissement | Décision et justification enregistrées |
Consultation n’est pas approbation. Relire un dessin ne signifie pas accepter le risque. Si l’autorité manque, la décision est bloquée plutôt qu’attribuée au premier ingénieur disponible.

## 2.9 Préoccupations en conflit
La continuité de C-04 peut favoriser l’activité locale ; l’intégrité de C-02 une autorité centrale sur la version actuelle. Les deux sont légitimes.
| Conflit | Option | Avantage | Conséquence et autorité |
| Continuité et autorité unique | Brouillons locaux, validation en ligne | Pas de décision finale concurrente | Attente acceptée par le métier |
| Continuité et autorité unique | Décisions locales limitées | Actions sélectionnées possibles | Délégation et conflits décidés par politique et risques |
| Traçabilité et minimisation | Preuves définies et accès limité | Explication préservée | Conservation justifiée par propriétaire |
| Déploiement rapide et reprise | Pilote préalable | Risque limité | Couverture initiale réduite acceptée par sponsor |
L’exemple recommande toujours brouillons hors connexion et approbation finale en ligne, sous réserve d’acceptation du coût d’interruption. ZAF n’interdit pas universellement l’approbation hors connexion.
Conserver alternatives, hypothèses et déclencheur de revue dans la décision.

## 2.10 Points de vue et vues
Dans ZAF, un point de vue définit préoccupations traitées, conventions et décision soutenue. Une vue est la représentation effectivement produite pour un périmètre. Ces définitions sont éditoriales.
| ID | Acteurs et préoccupations | Vue | Décision |
| VP-01 Contexte | Sponsor et responsables | Frontière et échanges | Périmètre et dépendances |
| VP-02 Autorité | Responsables délégués ; C-02, C-05 | Parcours et états | Décision et correction |
| VP-03 Information | Finance et données ; C-03, C-05 | Sources et traçabilité | Sens et publication |
| VP-04 Continuité | Terrain et système ; C-01, C-04, C-06 | Parcours interrompu | Mode dégradé et reprise |
| VP-05 Changement | Sponsor et réalisation | Dépendances et passages | Séquence d’investissement |
Chaque vue indique sujet, version, périmètre, légende, sources, auteur, questions ouvertes et réviseurs attendus. Aucun dessin unique ne répond à toutes les préoccupations.

## 2.11 Traçabilité
{{figure:traceability}}
Relier préoccupation, preuve, décision, vue et vérification permet d’expliquer une recommandation et ce qui la ferait changer.
| Préoccupation | Inconnu ou preuve | Décision proposée | Vue | Vérification |
| C-01 | Résultat ambigu | DEC-01 : réception stable et état explicite | VP-04 | Reprise d’une soumission |
| C-02 | Version non liée | DEC-02 : approbation sur version examinée | VP-02 | Refus après modification |
| C-03 | Période non convenue | DEC-03 : contrat versionné | VP-03 | Rapprochement connu |
| C-06 | Durée de reprise inconnue | DEC-04 : objectifs puis exercice | VP-04 | Restauration chronométrée |
Une inconnue est traçable lorsqu’elle indique ce qu’il faut apprendre ; elle ne doit pas apparaître comme une vérification achevée.

## 2.12 Plan de découverte
Organiser la collecte autour des décisions. L’entretien décrit la pratique voulue ; l’observation montre le parcours ; les documents permis permettent d’examiner une affirmation.
| Activité | Objet | Traitement | Livrable |
| Atelier de mandat | Autorité et périmètre | Notes approuvées | Frontière et responsables |
| Parcours | Réussites et refus | Échantillons expurgés ou synthétiques | Carte et exceptions |
| Sources et rapports | Expliquer un résultat | Données minimales autorisées | Définitions et rapprochement |
| Dépendances | Obligations fournisseurs | Extraits autorisés | Dépendances et escalade |
| Continuité | Coupures et reprise | Historique permis et exercices isolés | Hypothèses et lacunes |
Pour chaque activité : participant, autorisation, preuve, traitement, limite et décision soutenue. Aucun test intrusif ni export incontrôlé n’en découle automatiquement.
Justifier la couverture retenue, les exclusions et les limites de généralisation.

## 2.13 Incertitude et changement
| Contexte | Statut dans l’exemple | Décision affectée | Déclencheur |
| Connectivité | Coupures supposées | Continuité locale | Mesure différente |
| Équipe | Petite équipe supposée | Complexité plateforme | Responsabilités ou personnel changent |
| Localisation | Décision institutionnelle ouverte | Hébergement | Politique approuvée évolue |
| Reprise | Objectifs candidats | Sauvegarde et déploiement | Impact ou exercice modifie la faisabilité |
Un propriétaire suit chaque déclencheur important. Une revue annuelle ne remplace pas la réévaluation après un changement matériel.

## 2.14 Pièces et passage de revue
| Identifiant | Pièce | Preuve de revue |
| ZAF-I-02-A01 | Modèle de contexte | Frontières et propriétaires externes explicites |
| ZAF-I-02-A02 | Registre des acteurs | Représentation et autorité identifiées |
| ZAF-I-02-A03 | Registre des préoccupations | Décisions et statut des constats liés |
| ZAF-I-02-A04 | Catalogue de vues | Préoccupations et limites nommées |
| ZAF-I-02-A05 | Plan de découverte | Collecte autorisée et proportionnée |
| ZAF-I-02-A06 | Conflits et décisions | Options, propriétaires et arbitrages visibles |
| ZAF-I-02-A07 | Changements et dépendances | Déclencheurs et responsables enregistrés |
Le passage ne demande pas la disparition de toute inconnue. Les inconnues matérielles ont un responsable, une activité d’apprentissage et une restriction de décision.

## 2.15 Liste de revue et suite
- Frontières institutionnelle, de service et technique distinguées.
- Activités incluses et exclusions explicites.
- Terrain et utilisateurs représentés avec les autorités.
- Préoccupations sourcées et reliées aux conséquences.
- Consultation, correction des faits et acceptation distinguées.
- Conflits avec alternatives et escalade.
- Points de vue reliés aux préoccupations.
- Collecte autorisée et proportionnée.
- Hypothèses et couverture limitée visibles.
- Déclencheurs de changement attribués.
- Section 01 référencée sans approbation supposée.
- Pièces identifiées et vérifiables.
La section suivante est Finalité, valeur et résultats institutionnels. Elle utilisera ce contexte pour définir résultats, chaînes de valeur et limites de mesure. La section 02 reste un brouillon ; revue, constats et décisions réels seront enregistrés avant promotion de son statut.
